In [[set theory]], a subset of a [[Polish space]] <math>X</math> is '''∞-Borel''' if it
can be obtained by starting with the [[open set|open subsets]] of <math>X</math>, and [[transfinite recursion|transfinitely iterating]] the operations of [[Complement (set theory)|complementation]] and [[well-ordered]] [[Union (set theory)|union]]. This concept is usually considered without the assumption of the [[axiom of choice]], which means that the ∞-Borel sets may fail to be closed under well-ordered union; see below.

==Formal definition==
We define the set of '''∞-Borel codes''' <math>C</math> and the '''interpretation function''' <math>\left\| - \right\| : C \to \mathcal{P}(X)</math> below. A '''∞-Borel set''' is a subset of <math>X</math> which is in the image of the interpretation function <math>\left\| - \right\|</math>.

The set of ∞-Borel codes is an [[inductive type]] <math>C</math> generated by functions <math>\mathtt{open}: \mathcal{O}(X) \to C</math>, <math>\mathtt{comp} : C \to C</math> and <math>\mathtt{union}_\alpha : C^\alpha \to C</math> for each <math>\alpha < \Xi</math>; the interpretation function is defined inductively as <math>\left\| \mathtt{open}(U) \right\| = U</math>, <math>\left\| \mathtt{comp}(c) \right\| = X \setminus \left\| c \right\|</math> and <math>\left\| \mathtt{union}_\alpha(\vec c) \right\| = \cup_{\beta<\alpha}\left\| c_\beta \right\|</math>. Here <math>\Xi</math> denotes the [[Hartogs number]] of <math>\mathcal{P}(X)</math>: a sufficiently large [[ordinal number|ordinal]] such that there is no injection from <math>\Xi</math> to <math>\mathcal{P}(X)</math>. Restricting to unions of length below <math>\Xi</math> doesn't affect the possible unions (as any union of length <math> \geq \Xi </math> can be replaced by one of length <math> < \Xi </math> by removing duplicates), but ensures that the ∞-Borel codes form a set, not a [[proper class]].

This can be phrased more set-theoretically as a definition by [[transfinite recursion]] as follows:

* For every open subset <math>U \subseteq X</math>, the ordered pair <math>\left\langle 0,U\right\rangle</math> is an ∞-Borel code; its interpretation is <math>U</math>.
* If <math>c</math> is an ∞-Borel code, then the [[ordered pair]] <math>\left\langle 1,c\right\rangle</math> is also an ∞-Borel code; its interpretation is the complement of <math>\left\| c \right\|</math>, that is, <math>X \setminus \left\| c \right\|</math>.
* If <math>\vec c</math> is a length-α [[sequence]] of ∞-Borel codes for some ordinal α < Ξ (that is, if for every β<α, <math>c_\beta</math> is an ∞-Borel code), then the ordered pair <math>\left\langle 2,\vec c\right\rangle</math> is an ∞-Borel code; its interpretation is <math>\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}\left\| c_{\beta} \right\|</math>.

The axiom of choice implies that ''every'' set can be well-ordered, and therefore that every subset of every Polish space is ∞-Borel.  Therefore, the notion is interesting only in contexts where the axiom of choice does not hold (or is not known to hold). Unfortunately, without the axiom of choice, it is not clear that the ∞-Borel sets ''are'' closed under well-ordered union.  This is because, given a well-ordered union of ∞-Borel sets, each of the individual sets may have ''many'' ∞-Borel codes, and there may be no way to choose one code for each of the sets, with which to form the code for the union.

The assumption that every set of reals is ∞-Borel is part of [[AD plus|AD<sup>+</sup>]], an extension of the [[axiom of determinacy]] studied by [[W. Hugh Woodin|Woodin]].

==Incorrect definition==
It is very tempting to read the informal description at the top of this article as claiming that the ∞-Borel sets are the smallest class of subsets of <math>X</math> containing all the open sets and closed under complementation and well-ordered union.  That is, one might wish to dispense with the ∞-Borel codes altogether and try a definition like this:

: For each ordinal &alpha; define by transfinite recursion B<sub>&alpha;</sub> as follows:

:# B<sub>0</sub> is the collection of all [[open set|open subsets]] of <math>X</math>.
:# For a given [[even ordinal]] &alpha;, B<sub>&alpha;+1</sub> is the union of B<sub>&alpha;</sub> with the set of all [[Complement (set theory)|complements]] of sets in B<sub>&alpha;</sub>.
:# For a given even ordinal &alpha;, B<sub>&alpha;+2</sub> is the set of all [[well-ordered]] [[Union (set theory)|unions]] of sets in B<sub>&alpha;+1</sub>.
:# For a given [[limit ordinal]] &lambda;, B<sub>&lambda;</sub> is the union of all B<sub>&alpha;</sub> for &alpha;<&lambda;

: B<sub>&beta;</sub> equals B<sub>&Xi;</sub> for every &beta;>&Xi;; B<sub>&Xi;</sub> would then be the collection of "∞-Borel sets".

This set is manifestly closed under well-ordered unions, but without the axiom of choice it cannot be proved equal to the ∞-Borel sets (as defined in the previous section). Specifically, this set may contain unions of sequences <math>\vec b</math> of ∞-Borel sets for which it is not possible to choose a code for each <math>b_\beta</math>; it is the closure of the ∞-Borel sets under ''all'' well-ordered unions (and complements), even those for which a choice of codes cannot be made.

==Alternative characterization==
For subsets of [[Baire space (set theory)|Baire space]] or [[Cantor space]], there is a more concise (if less transparent) alternative definition, which turns out to be equivalent.  A subset ''A'' of Baire space is ∞-Borel just in case there is a set of ordinals ''S'' and a first-order formula ''φ'' of the [[language of set theory]] such that, for every ''x'' in Baire space,

: <math>x\in A\iff L[S,x]\models\phi(S,x)</math>

where ''L''[''S'',''x''] is [[Gödel's constructible universe#Relative constructibility|Gödel's constructible universe relativized]] to ''S'' and ''x''. When using this definition, the ∞-Borel code is made up of the set ''S'' and the formula ''φ'', taken together.
